polities.name: Delhi Sultanate
polities.summary: From the soaring Qutb Minar to the ramparts of Tughlaqabad, Delhi's sultans ruled the largest empire India had seen since the Mauryas, with Alauddin Khalji repelling Mongol invasions and raiding deep into the Deccan. Under Muhammad bin Tughluq the sultanate reached its greatest extent before Bengal broke away in 1352 and Timur's devastating sack of Delhi in 1398 left it a shadow of itself. Visit the Qutb complex, Alauddin's Siri Fort and Alai Darwaza, and Firuz Shah Kotla for this era in stone.

polities.name: Kakatiya Kingdom
polities.summary: The Kakatiyas ruled the Telugu country from mighty Warangal Fort, and were famously led by Rudrama Devi, one of medieval India's very few female sovereigns. Their engineers built vast irrigation tanks and the UNESCO-listed Ramappa Temple with its floating bricks. The kingdom fell to a Delhi Sultanate siege in 1323, after which the Musunuri Nayaks and Reddis of Kondavidu carried on Telugu rule.

polities.name: Yadavas of Devagiri
polities.summary: From the near-impregnable hill fortress of Devagiri, the Yadavas ruled the Marathi-speaking Deccan and patronized early Marathi literature and the saint-poet Dnyaneshwar. Alauddin Khalji's surprise raid of 1296 launched Delhi's push into the south, and the dynasty was extinguished by 1317. Today the fort, renamed Daulatabad, is one of Maharashtra's most dramatic day trips near Ellora.

polities.name: Hoysala Kingdom
polities.summary: The Hoysalas covered southern Karnataka with jewel-like star-shaped temples whose soapstone carvings at Belur, Halebidu and Somanathapura are now UNESCO World Heritage sites. Veera Ballala III fought the Delhi invasions for decades before dying in battle around 1343. From the wreckage of his kingdom rose Vijayanagara, founded in 1336 on the Tungabhadra by the brothers Harihara I and Bukka I, while the Bahmani Sultanate (founded 1347) claimed the northern Deccan.

polities.name: Pandya Empire of Madurai
polities.summary: Thirteenth-century Madurai was the glittering heart of the Tamil country, its pearl fisheries and spice ports praised by Marco Polo, and its Meenakshi Amman Temple the city's living centrepiece. Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I carried Pandya power to its peak, gilding temple roofs from Srirangam to Chidambaram. A succession war invited Delhi's raids, the short-lived Madurai Sultanate followed in 1335, and Vijayanagara absorbed the region by 1378.

polities.name: Venad (Later Chera) Kingdom
polities.summary: On Kerala's spice coast, the Venad kings ruled from the great pepper port of Kollam, where Chinese junks and Arab dhows met and travellers like Marco Polo and Ibn Battuta called. Ravi Varma Kulasekhara, a poet-king and author of a Sanskrit drama, even briefly conquered Madurai and crowned himself emperor of the south. His trading kingdom laid the foundations of later Travancore.

polities.name: Eastern Ganga Kingdom
polities.summary: The Eastern Gangas kept Odisha independent while northern India fell to the sultans, and celebrated their victories in stone: Narasimhadeva I built the colossal Konark Sun Temple, a chariot of the sun god with twelve carved wheels, now a UNESCO World Heritage site. The dynasty also lavished patronage on the Jagannath Temple at Puri, still one of India's greatest pilgrimage destinations.

polities.name: Ahom Kingdom
polities.summary: In 1228 the Tai prince Sukaphaa crossed the Patkai hills into the Brahmaputra valley and founded the Ahom kingdom, a dynasty that would rule Assam for nearly 600 years. His capital at Charaideo remained the sacred coronation and burial ground of Ahom kings, and its pyramid-like royal mounds, the Moidams, are now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Assam still celebrates Sukaphaa every December on Asom Divas.

polities.name: Kingdom of Mewar
polities.summary: Chittorgarh, one of India's largest hill forts and a UNESCO World Heritage site, was the stage for Alauddin Khalji's famous 1303 siege, forever linked to the legend of Rani Padmini. In 1326 Rana Hammir Singh recaptured the fort, founded the Sisodia line and restored Rajput rule in Mewar. His resurgent kingdom set Rajasthan's tradition of defiance that later Ranas would make legendary.

polities.name: Kashmir Sultanate
polities.summary: In 1339 Shah Mir supplanted the last Hindu Lohara rulers and founded Kashmir's first sultanate, beginning a new chapter for the valley. The era gave Srinagar its distinctive wooden mosque architecture, including the Khanqah-e-Moula shrine on the Jhelum, as Sufi saints like Shah-e-Hamadan shaped Kashmiri culture. The dynasty ruled the valley into the sixteenth century.

polities.name: Vijayanagara Empire
polities.dynasty: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva and Aravidu dynasties
polities.summary: For two centuries Vijayanagara ruled virtually the whole of South India from Hampi, a boulder-strewn capital of temples, bazaars and elephant stables that awed Persian and Portuguese visitors and is now a UNESCO World Heritage site. Under Krishnadevaraya, patron of Telugu poets and builder of the Vitthala Temple's stone chariot, the empire reached its golden age. After the catastrophic defeat at Talikota in 1565 the city was sacked, and its governors, the Nayaks of Madurai and Thanjavur, carried the legacy onward.

polities.name: Bahmani Sultanate and the Deccan Sultanates
polities.dynasty: Bahmani; then Adil Shahi (Bijapur), Qutb Shahi (Golconda), Nizam Shahi (Ahmadnagar), Imad Shahi (Berar), Barid Shahi (Bidar)
polities.capital: Gulbarga, then Bidar; later Bijapur, Golconda and Ahmadnagar
polities.summary: The Bahmani Sultanate, Vijayanagara's great rival across the Deccan, ruled from Gulbarga and then Bidar, whose fort and Persian-style madrasa of Mahmud Gawan still stand. Around 1490-1518 it splintered into five sultanates - Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Berar and Bidar - which united just once, to crush Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565. Their legacy includes the diamond-trading fortress of Golconda and the Charminar, built in 1591 as the centrepiece of newly founded Hyderabad.

polities.name: Mughal Empire
polities.capital: Agra and Delhi (later Fatehpur Sikri, Lahore)
polities.summary: Babur's victory at the First Battle of Panipat in 1526 founded the Mughal Empire, though his son Humayun was driven out by Sher Shah Suri, whose brilliant interregnum (1540-1555) gave India the Grand Trunk Road and his magnificent tomb at Sasaram in Bihar. Akbar rebuilt and vastly expanded the empire, annexing Gujarat, Bengal and Kashmir and preaching tolerance from his red-sandstone city of Fatehpur Sikri. Humayun's Tomb in Delhi, the garden-tomb that inspired the Taj Mahal, is the era's UNESCO-listed masterpiece.

polities.name: Delhi Sultanate (Sayyid and Lodi dynasties)
polities.summary: After Timur's sack, a shrunken Delhi Sultanate passed to the Sayyids and then the Afghan Lodis, who rebuilt power across the Gangetic plain and absorbed the Sharqi sultanate of Jaunpur, famed for its monumental mosques. Sikandar Lodi founded Agra as his capital in 1504, setting the stage for its Mughal glory. The dynasty's domed tombs give Delhi's Lodi Gardens their romance, and Ibrahim Lodi's death at Panipat in 1526 ended the sultanate forever.

polities.name: Gujarat Sultanate
states: Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu
polities.summary: Ahmad Shah I founded Ahmedabad in 1411, today India's first UNESCO World Heritage City, filled with exquisite stone-latticed mosques like the Sidi Saiyyed Jali. Mahmud Begada, conqueror of the twin forts of Junagadh and Pavagadh, presided over the sultanate's golden age and built the abandoned royal city of Champaner, another UNESCO site. The Portuguese seized Diu in 1535 and Daman in 1559, and Akbar annexed the sultanate in 1573.

polities.name: Malwa Sultanate
polities.dynasty: Ghurid (Malwa) and Khalji of Malwa dynasties
polities.summary: The sultans of Malwa turned the hilltop fortress city of Mandu into 'Shadiabad', the City of Joy, whose Jahaz Mahal seems to float like a ship between two lakes. Hoshang Shah's white marble tomb there is said to have inspired the builders of the Taj Mahal. The romance of its last sultan Baz Bahadur and the singer Rani Roopmati still haunts Mandu's pavilions; Akbar annexed the kingdom in 1562.

polities.name: Bengal Sultanate
polities.dynasty: Ilyas Shahi and Hussain Shahi dynasties
polities.summary: Independent of Delhi since 1352, the Bengal Sultanate grew rich on rice, muslin and river trade, and its capital Gaur was among the most populous cities on earth. Under Alauddin Hussain Shah, Bengali literature flourished and the mystic Chaitanya Mahaprabhu began his devotional movement. The atmospheric brick ruins of Gaur and Pandua, near Malda, preserve its distinctive terracotta mosque architecture; the Mughals absorbed Bengal in 1576.

polities.name: Gajapati Empire
polities.summary: Kapilendra Deva, a soldier who seized the throne in 1435, forged the Gajapati Empire that stretched from the Ganga to the Kaveri, making Odisha the great Hindu power of eastern India. The dynasty were devoted patrons of the Jagannath Temple at Puri, and the saint Chaitanya spent his last years there under Prataparudra Deva. Cuttack's Barabati Fort and Puri's living temple traditions recall Odisha's imperial age.

polities.name: Kingdom of Mewar
polities.summary: This was Mewar's heroic age: Rana Kumbha built the massive Kumbhalgarh fort, whose 36-kilometre wall is among the longest on earth, and raised the Vijay Stambha victory tower at Chittorgarh - both UNESCO-listed hill forts of Rajasthan. Rana Sanga united the Rajputs and nearly toppled Babur before falling at Khanwa in 1527. After Akbar sacked Chittor in 1568, Udai Singh II's new lake city of Udaipur became the capital, and Maharana Pratap's defiance at Haldighati in 1576 made him a legend.

polities.name: Portuguese India (Estado da India)
polities.summary: Vasco da Gama's landing at the Zamorin of Calicut's shore in 1498 opened the sea route from Europe, and in 1510 Afonso de Albuquerque seized Goa from Bijapur, making it the capital of Portugal's Asian empire. Old Goa grew into the 'Rome of the East', its UNESCO-listed churches including the Basilica of Bom Jesus, resting place of St. Francis Xavier. Portuguese forts at Cochin, Daman and Diu still dot the western seaboard, alongside the spice kingdoms of the Zamorin and Cochin they traded and warred with.
